_metadata.note: split from waymo_gt_verified.json known-absent arm (REAL absent facts, not fabricated entities) for RI-M7 census
_metadata.description: Cross-verified union of the two independently-authored Waymo AV-safety ground-truth sets (GT-A from oxalpha, GT-B from claude), built by ticket GT-X. Only items that survived mechanical excerpt-fidelity checking, independent absence re-verification, answerability review, and numeric grounding audit are included.
_metadata.verification_method: Every grounding claim re-checked read-only against waymo/data/papers.db (1,738 papers / 46,155 chunks as of 2026-08-19 mtime): paper existence and title, chunk-to-paper membership, anchor_json block-id agreement, whitespace-normalized substring containment of every excerpt (primary and supporting), section-path agreement, numeral-level audit of every answer_text against the cited paper's text. All 8 absent items re-searched independently with additional adversarial probes beyond the authors' own logs. Full findings and ruled near-misses: docs/eval-reports/2026-08-22-waymo-groundtruth-cross-verification.md.
_metadata.dimension_labels_note: The two source sets use partially different dimension vocabularies (GT-A short forms e.g. 'numeric/quantitative'; GT-B noun forms e.g. 'numeric/quantitative claims'). Labels are preserved verbatim per item rather than normalized -- normalizing them here would silently rewrite the authors' labels; consumers should group via the mapping in the report if they need one bucketing.
known_caveats: Q-WAYB-027 is vision-derived: only its machine-checkable ids/page were verified; the visual claim itself is unverified by the cross-verifier.

Several GT-B absence_search logs record hit counts that do not reproduce under plain SQLite LIKE on the frozen DB (see per-item verification.notes); every qualitative absence nevertheless held up under independent re-search.

ground_truth.question_text: What LiDAR wavelength does Waymo's autonomous-driving hardware platform use, according to the corpus's own papers?
ground_truth.absence_note: The corpus contains many Waymo-authored papers describing perception, detection, and safety-performance results, but none of them discloses a specific LiDAR wavelength for Waymo's own sensor hardware -- Waymo's papers describe point-cloud data and detection algorithms without disclosing this kind of proprietary hardware spec. This is a plausible-sounding, in-domain question (hardware questions are common in AV papers) whose answer is genuinely not in this corpus.
absence_search: chunks.text LIKE '%wavelength%' (10 hits total across the whole 1,738-paper corpus; none discuss a Waymo-specific LiDAR wavelength -- hits are unrelated papers on MHD turbulence, lattice-Boltzmann simulation, V2X signal models, etc.)

papers.title LIKE '%LiDAR%' spot-checked among the 153 Waymo-authored paper_ids for hardware-spec disclosures (e.g. 2005.08417-style sensor papers are absent from this corpus; the Waymo-authored LiDAR papers here, e.g. 2106.13365 RSN, 2103.01306, are all about detection algorithms over already-released point clouds, not sensor hardware specs)
ground_truth.provenance: absence established by keyword search over chunks.text (papers.db) for 'wavelength' across the full corpus, and by spot-checking the Waymo-authored LiDAR-adjacent paper set for any hardware-spec disclosure; see absence_search

notes: Absence verdict confirmed, but the recorded search-log hit count does not reproduce: 'wavelength' matches 35 chunks across 20 papers under plain SQLite LIKE today, not the 10 recorded. None of the hits discloses a Waymo-hardware LiDAR wavelength, so the qualitative absence stands. Adversarial probes ('1550', '1550 nm', 'lidar wavelength') found only camera-resolution tables and unrelated FMCW physics.

ground_truth.question_text: How many pedestrian, cyclist, and vehicle-occupant fatalities has Waymo's driverless fleet caused in total, broken down by category, according to the corpus's papers?
ground_truth.absence_note: The corpus contains several Waymo-authored and third-party retrospective crash-rate studies (7.1M, 25.3M, 56.7M mile mileposts) that discuss injury severity tiers up to 'Suspected Serious Injury+', and other papers that discuss AV fatalities in the aggregate (e.g. human benchmark fatal-crash rates per 100 million miles), but none of the Waymo-specific studies in this corpus reports a specific Waymo-attributed fatality count broken down by victim category. This is a plausible, in-domain question (fatality counts are exactly the kind of headline number these papers report for lower-severity outcomes) whose specific answer is not present.
absence_search: chunks.text LIKE '%fatal%' restricted to chunks whose text or title also mentions 'waymo' (23 of 200 sampled 'fatal' hits corpus-wide); manual review of all 23 found no Waymo-attributed fatality count -- hits are either about human benchmark fatality rates, unrelated papers' introductions, or Waymo safety-case papers discussing severity thresholds in the abstract without a concrete count
chunks.text LIKE '%fatality involving%' (0 hits relevant to Waymo)
ground_truth.provenance: absence established by keyword search over chunks.text (papers.db) for 'fatal' co-occurring with 'waymo', plus targeted phrase searches; see absence_search

notes: Absence verdict confirmed by re-search: 430 'fatalit*' chunk hits corpus-wide, 29 of them co-occurring with 'waymo' reviewed individually (human benchmarks, severity-tier discussion, mission statements) plus death/died/killed/deaths probes; none reports a Waymo-attributed fatality count broken down by victim category.

ground_truth.question_text: What is the reported disengagement rate per 1,000 miles specifically for Waymo's 5th-generation ('Gen 5') hardware platform, as distinct from its 4th-generation platform, according to the corpus?
ground_truth.absence_note: The corpus's disengagement-related papers (e.g. 'Initial Indications of Safety of Driverless Automated Driving Systems', which uses California DMV disengagement reporting) discuss disengagement data in aggregate across companies/time periods, not broken down by Waymo's own internal hardware-generation labels. No paper in the corpus reports a hardware-generation-specific disengagement rate for Waymo.
absence_search: chunks.text LIKE '%disengagement%' (10 hits corpus-wide; none mention a hardware-generation breakdown for any single ADS operator)
chunks.text LIKE '%5th-generation%' / '%fifth generation%' / '%Gen 5%' -- no hits describing a Waymo hardware-generation-specific safety metric

chunks.text LIKE '%hardware platform%' (5 hits corpus-wide, all about other systems' compute hardware -- NVIDIA DriveAV, Apollo/Nuvo-6108GC, AD-EYE co-simulation rigs -- not a Waymo generation-specific disengagement rate)
ground_truth.provenance: absence established by keyword search over chunks.text (papers.db) for 'disengagement', hardware-generation phrasings, and 'hardware platform'; see absence_search

notes: Absence verdict confirmed, but the recorded search-log hit count does not reproduce: 'disengagement' matches 168 chunks across 75 papers today, not the 10 recorded. No hit gives a hardware-generation-specific disengagement rate for any single operator, so the qualitative absence stands.

ground_truth.question_text: What statistical power analysis did the RAVE Checklist's working group perform to empirically validate that following its fifteen recommendations improves the accuracy of retrospective ADS safety studies?
ground_truth.absence_note: The RAVE Checklist is a consensus recommendations paper produced by an expert working group (established via in-person and virtual meetings, per its own Methods section) -- it is not an empirical study, and it does not report any power analysis or other quantitative validation of its own recommendations' effect on study accuracy. The paper does discuss statistical power as a concept researchers should consider when choosing severity outcomes (its 'statistically significant conclusions' / severity-level guidance), but that is advice given to other researchers, not a self-validation of the checklist.
absence_search: chunks.text LIKE '%power analysis%' restricted to paper_id='local:4087ccce4c01' (0 hits)

chunks.text LIKE '%statistical power%' restricted to the same paper_id (2 hits: local:4087ccce4c01:c20 and :c22, both guidance to future researchers about severity-level statistical power, not a validation of the checklist itself)
full chunk-by-chunk read of the paper's Methods/Results/Conclusions sections (local:4087ccce4c01:c3/c4/c5/c25) -- describes a working-group consensus process, not an empirical validation study
ground_truth.provenance: absence established by targeted phrase search over chunks.text restricted to this paper_id, plus a full read of its Methods/Results/Conclusions chunks

ground_truth.question_text: What blinding procedure does Waymo's Fatigue Risk Management Framework paper use to prevent evaluator bias when assessing autonomous specialists' fatigue survey responses?
ground_truth.absence_note: This paper is a proposed policy/framework document (prevention, monitoring, and mitigation practices for fatigue risk), not a randomized or blinded empirical study, and it contains no discussion of blinding at all. This is a plausible-sounding methodological question (blinding is a standard concern for survey-based assessments) whose premise -- that a blinding procedure exists in this paper -- is false.
absence_search: chunks.text LIKE '%blind%' / '%blinded%' / '%blinding%' restricted to paper_id='2208.12833' (0 hits for all three)
ground_truth.provenance: absence established by phrase search over chunks.text restricted to this paper_id; see absence_search

ground_truth.question_text: Which paper in this corpus reports Zoox's own crashes-per-million-mile safety performance figure from a dedicated Zoox safety study?
ground_truth.absence_note: Zoox appears in this corpus only as one of several companies named in a third-party aggregate comparison (2403.14648, which pools DMV/CPUC-reported mileage and crash data across Waymo, Cruise, Lyft, and Zoox) -- there is no paper in the corpus, Waymo-authored or otherwise, that presents a dedicated, Zoox-specific crash-rate benchmark study analogous to Waymo's 7.1M/25.3M/56.7M-mile self-studies. This is a plausible in-domain question (the corpus is full of exactly this kind of company-specific benchmark paper for Waymo) whose premise -- that an equivalent Zoox-specific paper exists -- is false.
absence_search: chunks.text LIKE '%Zoox%' (11 hits across the whole corpus); manual review shows all 11 are passing mentions of Zoox as one of several companies in aggregate comparison tables/text (chiefly 2403.14648), none is itself a Zoox-dedicated safety-performance study
ground_truth.provenance: absence established by title search and full-text keyword search over papers.db; see absence_search

notes: Absence verdict confirmed: 0 title hits; 11 Zoox chunk mentions across 10 papers (matching the recorded count), all passing mentions -- aggregate comparisons, a disengagement-rate remark citing Zoox's own historical claim, incident anecdotes, and one Zoox-authored validation-methodology paper (2411.03328). None is a dedicated Zoox crashes-per-million-mile safety-performance study.

ground_truth.question_text: Using the same underreporting-adjusted police-reported human benchmark rate (the Blincoe-adjusted rate) that Waymo's 7.1-million-mile rider-only crash study used, what crash-rate reduction did Cruise achieve when evaluated against that identical benchmark?
ground_truth.absence_note: Waymo's 7.1-million-mile and 25.3-million-mile self-studies compare Waymo's own rider-only data to human benchmarks (including a Blincoe et al.-adjusted police-reported rate); neither paper computes or reports an equivalent figure for Cruise against that same benchmark. The only paper in this corpus that discusses Cruise's own crash rate (2403.14648) uses a different benchmark methodology entirely (raw DMV/CPUC mileage and crash counts, compared to Uber TNC human driving in San Francisco), not the Blincoe-adjusted police-reported rate. No paper cross-applies Waymo's specific benchmark methodology to Cruise's data.
absence_search: chunks.text LIKE '%Cruise%' restricted to paper_id IN ('2312.12675','local:6b9ccd0431f6','local:f6f1461f2c9a') (2 hits total, both in 2312.12675:c11 and local:f6f1461f2c9a:c4 -- both are literature-review-style mentions of prior benchmark methodology discussions, not a Cruise-specific reduction figure computed against Waymo's benchmark)

full read of 2403.14648 (the only paper in the corpus computing an actual Cruise crash-rate figure) confirms it uses DMV/CPUC raw mileage and Uber TNC comparison data, not the Blincoe-adjusted police-reported benchmark used in Waymo's own 7.1M/25.3M-mile papers
ground_truth.provenance: absence established by keyword search over chunks.text restricted to the three Waymo self-authored crash-rate papers, plus a full read of 2403.14648's methodology; see absence_search

notes: Absence verdict confirmed, but it is a near miss worth flagging: 2312.12675:c11 does report a Cruise-specific reduction (Zhang 2023: 65%, any-property-damage-or-injury, first 1M Cruise RO miles) -- however it was computed against the Flannagan et al. (2023) ride-hailing NDS benchmark, NOT the Blincoe-adjusted police-reported rate the question names, so the question as asked remains unanswerable from this corpus.

ground_truth.question_text: What crash-rate reduction figures did Waymo report in a rider-only crash-rate study at the 100-million-mile milestone?
ground_truth.absence_note: Waymo's rider-only crash-rate research program in this corpus has published results at 7.1 million miles (2312.12675), 25.3 million miles for the insurance-claims variant (local:f6f1461f2c9a), and 56.7 million miles (local:6b9ccd0431f6, the most recent/largest of the series, through end of January 2025) -- there is no 100-million-mile report in this corpus. This is a plausible extrapolation (the series clearly grows over time) but no such milestone report exists here.
absence_search: chunks.text LIKE '%100 million miles%' / '%100.0 million%' / '%100-million-mile%' across the whole corpus -- hits found are all in unrelated papers (a 2016-era formal-verification paper's passing remark that 'driverless tests from Waymo and Tesla range around 100 million miles' at time of writing, a fatal-crash-rate-per-100-million-miles national statistic, and an accelerated-evaluation paper's rhetorical illustration) -- none is a Waymo rider-only crash-rate report at that mileage
confirmed the three Waymo RO crash-rate self-studies in the corpus cap out at 56.7 million miles (through end of January 2025), the largest mileage figure found in any of their abstracts
ground_truth.provenance: absence established by phrase search over chunks.text across the whole corpus; see absence_search

notes: Absence verdict confirmed, but the recorded search log is incomplete: it missed the strongest 100-million-mile hit in the corpus, 2507.17943:c2 ('quickly reached 100 million miles in July 2025'), which the parallel GT-A set uses for its timeline item Q-GTA-015. Adjudication: that is a cited mileage-milestone mention inside a brake-onset paper, not a rider-only crash-rate study at 100M miles reporting reduction figures, so this absence still stands under its precise wording.
